concept.name: Iceberg detection
concept.definition: The inference of iceberg orders — limit orders whose exchange-visible displayed size is only a small tip of a much larger hidden total — from market data. Because exchanges do not report the hidden size, detection algorithms watch for a displayed quote that keeps replenishing after executions, or trade volume at a price exceeding the displayed size.
concept.intuition: If the same 50-lot offer keeps reappearing after being hit and thousands of contracts trade through it, something much bigger is sitting below the waterline.
concept.mechanics: Track market-data dynamics rather than snapshots: with market-by-order data, new limit orders appearing instantly on the opposite side of executions at the same price reveal the reload; with lower-quality data, heuristics (trade size exceeding displayed size, repeated same-size refills) estimate it, always as an approximation.
concept.failure_modes: Detection is provably limited: hidden size and placement/cancellation moments cannot be observed, and data-vendor aggregation or channel splitting destroys the event sequence the algorithms depend on; high-frequency traders can also mimic icebergs with ordinary limit orders.
concept.misconceptions: A detected iceberg is not a guaranteed support/resistance wall — the owner can cancel instantly, and some large traders deliberately display iceberg-like behavior to mislead.
concept.example: The offer at 4,505 displays 100 lots; 2,400 contracts trade there while the display keeps refreshing at 100 — an iceberg tracker marks probable hidden selling, and the level holds as resistance.

citations.source: Bookmap Knowledge Base — Iceberg Orders Tracker
